html:
A trading land in the Persian Gulf, centred on the island of Bahrain, that served as the go-between for Mesopotamia and the lands to the east. It appears in cuneiform texts from the 3rd millennium BCE and was at its height around 2050 to 1800 BCE.

Ships from Dilmun carried copper from Magan in Oman and carnelian, ivory and timber from Meluhha, the Indus Valley, to Ur and the other Sumerian cities. Sargon of Akkad boasted that Dilmun's ships docked at his capital. Dilmun merchants used their own round stamp seals, and Bahrain holds tens of thousands of burial mounds from this time.

Sumerian myth called Dilmun a pure land where no one grew sick or old, and one flood story places the survivor there to live forever. After the Indus cities declined, Dilmun's trade shrank. It came under Kassite Babylon and later Assyria, and the name faded in the 1st millennium BCE.
